title: Other trumpeters said his tone was bad: Preston Jackson and the Spivak comparison
summary: When he arrived from Milwaukee, trumpeters knocked his tone; Preston Jackson heard him play and found nothing wrong, and Randolph says he played like Charlie Spivak.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Now, when I first came from Milwaukee here, all the trumpet players -- all the trumpet players knocked me. They knocked me so til one day Preston Jackson came over to my house. He says, "Well, Topsy, I know you used to play horn," that's what he called me sometimes --

Old Top, Old Top. He said, "Old Top, I know you used to play horn," he said, "But I done heard so much about your tone being so bad." He said, "Get your horn and play something for me. I just want to hear. I want to see for myself." You know, I had to convince him. I had the trumpet under my bed. I just reached and got the horn out and warmed up. And I played -- ba-da-la-la-la-di-di- And he said, "Ain't nothing the matter with your tone." He said the guys all said I had a nanny tone. Well, you know, that was jealous.
I tell you, looking back, the way I play -- you ever heard Spivak -- Charlie Spivak?
That's -- I had never heard Spivak do it, now, but since I have heard Spivak and looking back at the way I play -- I played more of a Spivak trumpet.
See? But I didn't copy him because

I didn't know there was a Spivak. But they all said they wanted me to play -- da-ta-ta-ta -- you know, just straight -- ta-ta-ta- but I don't care for my tone going that way. You don't sing that way. An instrument is supposed to play like you sing.
